title: Examination of the Agent and Action

slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter eight: the examination of the agent and action.

slides.heading: The baker and the baking
points: A baker, and the baking they do
The baker before and after the bread
slides.say: Someone bakes bread. There is a baker, and there is the baking, and the two seem easy to tell apart. The baker was there before the bread and will be there after it; the baking is something the baker does. Our whole idea of responsibility rests on this picture. Someone did it, and the deed is theirs.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: How are a doer and a deed related?
Then verse 8.12: each depends on the other
slides.say: This short chapter asks how a doer and a deed are related. It follows on from chapter two, where the goer and the going were found to be named together, and from chapter seven, where the three marks could not be found as things have them on their own. If the agent and the action each exist on their own, can one do the other? Nagarjuna tests every combination and finds that none works. Then, in one of the key verses of the whole text, verse eight point twelve, he says how they do go together: each is established only in dependence on the other.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Nine pairings
slides.say: Now the explanation. Two words carry the chapter. The agent is the one who acts. The action is what is done; here it means simply a deed, not yet the karma of rebirth, which comes in chapter seventeen. A third word matters too: really existing, meaning there already, complete and on its own. So the question is precise. Suppose the agent and the action are each a thing with its own existence, there before they meet. Can such an agent do such an action? There are three possibilities for each: really existing, not existing, or a mixture. That gives nine pairings, and Nagarjuna checks all of them. The three on the diagonal are argued in full; the other six inherit the same faults.

slides.heading: A real agent and a real action
points: A complete action needs no one to do it
A complete agent needs no action
Each complete in itself, they cannot meet
slides.say: Start with the common-sense case: a baker who really exists, on their own, and a baking that really exists, on its own. A baking that already exists, complete in itself, does not need anyone to do it. It is done. So it would be an action without an agent. And an agent already complete as an agent does not need an action to be one. So they would be a baker who never bakes. Something fully there from its own side cannot be in the middle of becoming anything. If the doer and the deed were each complete in themselves, they would not need each other, and so they could not meet in doing.

slides.heading: An unreal agent and action
slides.say: The opposite case fails more obviously. If an agent who does not exist did an action that does not exist, both would come from nothing, with no cause at all. Verses four to six follow this out. Without causes, there are no effects and no means. Without these, no activity and no agent. Without activity, no good or bad conduct. Without conduct, no fruit, no path to a good rebirth or to liberation, and every action in the world becomes pointless. This turns a familiar worry around. People fear that if the doer is empty, no one is responsible. Nagarjuna argues the reverse. It is the picture of self-standing agents and actions, or of actions from nothing, that would make conduct meaningless. He makes the same point at length in chapter twenty-four.

slides.heading: The mixed cases
points: Existing and not existing contradict each other
The other six pairings inherit the same faults
slides.say: Could the agent be a mixture, partly existing and partly not? Existing and not existing contradict each other. They cannot both be true of the same thing in the same respect, any more than a light can be both on and off. The remaining six pairings mix the cases, and each simply inherits the faults already found. A real agent still has nothing left to do; an unreal agent still has no cause; a mixed one is still self-contradictory. The verses say so briefly, for the reasons already given.

slides.heading: Named together
slides.say: After nine failures, verse twelve gives the way agent and action actually go together. The agent proceeds in dependence on the action, and the action in dependence on the agent. We see no other basis on which they could be established. Notice what this does not say. It does not say the action is real and the agent a mere label, nor that the agent is real and owns the action. Neither is the ground of the other. Someone is a baker because there is baking; something is baking because someone bakes. Is this a vicious circle? Only for someone who expects dependence to pass existence along from a starting point. Nagarjuna's point is that neither exists first. That is exactly why neither exists from its own side. The last verse widens the result: the one who grasps and the grasping go together in the same way, and every other pair is to be examined like agent and action.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: The baker still bakes, and the bread is theirs
Responsibility works better without a fixed doer
This is why practice is possible
slides.say: The baker still bakes, and the bread is theirs. We can still say who did what, praise good work and hold people to their promises. None of this needs an agent who exists on their own before acting. In fact, responsibility works better without one. An agent fixed in their own nature could not learn, regret or change. Because the agent is designated in dependence on what they do, a person who acts differently becomes, in a real sense, a different kind of agent. This is why practice is possible. What goes is only the hidden doer standing behind the doing, and the doing that floats free of anyone doing it.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Anatta to Emptiness: The Great Desynchronization
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: chapter eleven, on doing without a doer; chapter four, on why mutual dependence is not a vicious circle; and chapter nine, on who is responsible if no one persists. In The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness, the chapter on the great desynchronization explains why no action without an agent does not bring back a self. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter nine, the examination of the prior entity.
